title: Loving children
hookLine: Gibran: your children come through you but are not from you (The Prophet, 1923)

lines: A POET AND AN OLDER STORY.
cards: On the inside of a kitchen doorframe, a column of pencil lines climbs toward the ceiling, each with a name and a date. Somebody stood very straight in socks while somebody else laid a book flat on their head.
The lines are a record of growth, and of something harder: every one marks a child getting a little further from needing the person holding the pencil.
A Lebanese-American poet wrote a short chapter about exactly that, and an older story says it without saying it.

teach.b: First, not your children. In Kahlil Gibran's book The Prophet, a woman holding a baby asks the prophet to speak of children. His first words are startling: "Your children are not your children."
He goes on: "They are the sons and daughters of Life's longing for itself." It sounds cold at first. It isn't.
A child is bigger than the plans anyone makes for them.
Second, through you, not from you. "They come through you but not from you," the prophet says. A parent is a doorway, not an owner.
And then: "You may give them your love but not your thoughts, For they have their own thoughts." A child's inner life is their own.
Third, the bow and the arrow. "You are the bows from which your children as living arrows are sent forth."

Gibran ends by asking the bow to bend gladly in the archer's hand, because the archer loves the bow that stays steady as much as the arrow that flies. The parent isn't sidelined; the parent makes the flight possible.

teach.h: A MOTHER KEEPS IT IN HER HEART.
teach.b: Fourth, a mother keeps it in her heart. In the Gospel of Luke, the boy Jesus stays behind in the temple, and his parents search for him for days.
When they find him, Mary says: "Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." The text says they didn't understand his answer.
And then, simply: "his mother kept all these sayings in her heart." She keeps his words without needing to master them.

how: Gibran's chapter 'On Children' is read aloud by some families and at some ceremonies; Christians tell the story of the boy Jesus in the temple from Luke 2.

o: love that shapes a child's thoughts to match yours
love that keeps a child close and never lets go
love that gives freely and holds a child loosely

games.q: who said what about children — tap the pairs.
p: your children are not your children
stays steady while the arrow flies
kept all these sayings in her heart

s: Gibran's prophet says children belong to their parents
they are with you, yet they belong not to you.
in Luke, Mary keeps the boy Jesus's puzzling words in her heart
his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.
the bow-and-arrow image means parents don't matter
the archer loves the steady bow as much as the flying arrow; the bow makes the flight possible.

games.q: you're the parent. your child loves something you'd never have chosen for them. what does Gibran's prophet advise?
o: steer them back to your plan.
let them be, and stay steady nearby.
step away and leave them to it.
games.why: you may strive to be like them, but seek not to make them like you. and the bow stays steady.

practice: Let a child come to mind, your own, a niece, a student, a neighbor's kid, or the child you once were, and see them as they actually are right now: what they love, what makes them laugh.

Notice one way they're different from what anyone expected, and instead of correcting it, let it be, and quietly wish them well in it, steady as the bow. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name.

wordCard.voice: Loving children. Love that gives freely and holds loosely, the way Gibran's prophet sees a parent as the bow and the child as the arrow. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: through you, not from you. The bow sends; the arrow flies. Day eight hundred sixty-three.
